# FSAE-Wake-Deflector
* The goal of this project is to design an aerodynamic wake deflector to manage the turbulent flow (“dirty air”) generated by the front tires of an FSAE car. This flow interferes with the undertray and side channel, reducing downforce and stability. The deflector aims to shield the side channel inlet from tire wake and to generate vortices that enhance undertray performance during both straight-line and cornering conditions.

## Fundamentals: 
- Open-wheel cars, including Formula SAE designs, suffer from highly turbulent flow around the front tires. As the tire rotates, the airflow separates along its shoulders, forming strong lateral vortices and a low-energy wake behind it. This unsteady, chaotic region—often called “dirty air”—contains low total pressure and high turbulence intensity.
When this wake interacts with the undertray or side channel inlet, it reduces the available clean flow that generates ground-effect downforce. In simple terms, the wake pollutes the undertray’s airflow, decreasing suction and stability.
### Flow Shielding and Redirection
- One approach to mitigating this is flow shielding, where an aerodynamic surface (such as a deflector wall) blocks or redirects the tire wake. However, this solution has limitations. A solid wall creates a stagnation zone on its upstream side and often leads to flow separation downstream, introducing drag and further turbulence.
Therefore, the better approach is flow redirection rather than pure blocking. By shaping the deflector with curvature or an airfoil profile, the air can be guided smoothly around the wake region, preserving flow energy and directing cleaner, higher-momentum air toward the undertray inlet.
### Vortex Generation and Control
- A more advanced strategy—used extensively in Formula 1—is vortex generation. Controlled vortices act like rotating tubes of high-energy air that can “seal” the underfloor, much like virtual skirts. The swirling motion of a vortex pulls faster air from above into the lower boundary layer, re-energizing it and delaying flow separation.
In the context of an FSAE car, the wake deflector can be designed with an airfoil-like geometry or sharp turning edge to induce a pressure difference between its suction and pressure sides. The rolling-up of flow at the deflector’s tip produces a coherent vortex that travels along the side channel, maintaining undertray suction.<br />
However, vortex behavior is highly sensitive to its environment. Its strength, trajectory, and longevity depend on:
  - Pressure gradient along its path.
  - Proximity to solid surfaces, which induce viscous shear.
  - Contamination by surrounding turbulence, such as tire wake.
### Viscous Dissipation and Vortex Decay
- Even if a strong vortex is generated at the inlet, it can decay rapidly due to viscous dissipation. This term describes how internal friction within the air (viscosity) converts the vortex’s organized rotational kinetic energy into heat and small-scale turbulence.
As the vortex interacts with the ground plane and side channel walls, shear layers form that gradually sap its energy. The higher the viscosity effects and turbulence intensity, the faster this decay occurs.
### Application to FSAE Scale
- At the FSAE scale, vortices are smaller and more sensitive to Reynolds number effects. This means they dissipate faster than in F1-scale aerodynamics, where higher speeds sustain coherent vortex structures. Therefore, achieving a long-lived vortex in FSAE requires careful balance: it must be strong enough to survive viscous losses, but not so aggressive that it causes flow separation or drag.
Reference: Willem Toet, “Motorsport Diffusers,” Racetech Magazine, 2017.
(https://www.racetechmag.com/2017/08/willem-toet-explains-motorsport-diffusers/)

### Constraint
  Because the deflector mounts around the A-arm and runs very close to the ground, the design uses a modular, multi-panel approach with localized doubler plates and through-bolt attachments to prevent fastener shear-out in the carbon-fiber honeycomb sandwich. Sacrificial UHMW skid strips and aramid-reinforced outer plies protect the laminate from abrasion and low-energy ground strikes; skids are bolted to backing plates so they are quickly replaceable. Fastener regions are either through-bolted to a backing plate or use bonded aluminum doublers with stainless steel threaded inserts to spread bearing loads and prevent core crush. All quick-release hardware is installed over doublers and captive nut plates to enable rapid service while preserving structural integrity. In order to test the mounting and the height of the deflector, we made flat plate deflector that is the same size as the curve ones, to see how much will scrap off and does the deflector survibe the impact.

## CFD Images of Baseline Design

- The baseline configuration was analyzed using CFD, focusing on total pressure (CPt) distribution. Lower CPt regions correspond to higher-speed flow, which is desirable in the undertray region.
The results show a vortex forming near the deflector and propagating toward the side channel inlet. The high-speed circular region in the CPt plot confirms vortex formation. However, the vortex weakens and dissipates before reaching the end of the side channel, indicating a loss of potential downforce. <br />


https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6df0616a-7128-4ec6-8536-f26ac41c4163


  
- In this video and  image we can see the vortex generated by the deflector and its position in relation to the side channel inlet by the looking at the CPt, see that there is a high air speed zone in a circular shape. As the vortex progress through the side channel we can see that it does not survibe at the lowest point of the side channel losing potential downforce being created, there are some assumption as to why this happend. 
     - The vortex core is too weak to survive the full channel length.
     - The channel geometry is too low, causing early vortex breakdown.
     - Insufficient clean flow enters the inlet, with some of the tire wake contaminating the vortex despite the deflector wall.
- In your baseline CFD, the observed weakening of the vortex near the outlet of the side channel can be explained by viscous dissipation combined with insufficient clean flow. The tire wake likely increases turbulence intensity at the inlet, causing the vortex core to diffuse and lose coherence before reaching the diffuser exit.
To counteract this, a stronger or more coherent vortex can be generated by:
Increasing the pressure differential across the deflector (via camber or higher angle of attack).
Providing clean, attached flow to the deflector leading edge.
Adjusting vortex placement so it travels through regions of favorable pressure gradient and minimal wall interference.

## Iteration 47 - 80++ ( This concept is still being develop and optimize)

  Due to the fact that the flat plate worked really well, I used that concept as a foundation. In order to create a strong vortex without pulling in the wake of the tire, I need to have the deflector closer to the chassis in order to position the vortex further from the tire wake. However this leave the side channel inlet open that allow the wake to enter the side channel. Thus why not have 2 deflector, one deflector will on the outside(outboard), smaller and place close to the tire in order to stop the wake from getting into the side channel and the second one (inboard) will be place closer to the chassis due to the front wing main plain provding clean airflow. 
  Futhermore what we can do it to generate a vortex that will lift the dirty air away from the side channel foot plate, thus providing the side channel with clean air that will add more energy and create more downforce. 
  Due to the fact that this element is mounted in the suspension geometry, there are certain area where airflow will be bad, thus we should try to ignore the suspension by making it taller than the geometry. Now to make the upper vortex stronger we need a more agressive curve, however if we were to increase the curve lenght or angle the wheels will hit the deflector while turning, this the upper part is shifted toward the chassis even more. so that even though the top and bottom will end at the same place, the agressiveness of the curvature will be different. 
  However due to the fact that the upper vortex is generated so high above the side channel the desire effect would be less effective this we need something to drag down the vortex. Thus we can use a lift generating airfoil in order to create a downwash effect that will drag the vortex down with it.

  As shown in the video, the outboard is controling the tire wake and preventing it from entering the side channel, not only that it is also creating a outwash that allow more clean air to enter the sidechannel later downstream. This allow the inboard to generate a powerful vortex that survive the entire side channel. Comparing to the baseline this set up was able to generate 40N+ in yaw and reduce the sensitivity from losing 11% of downforce from straight to a yaw angle of 6 to losing only 3%. 

  However there is a flaw to this design, due to the stronger upper vortex of the inboard it is actually pulling the tire wake and unwanted vortex from the front wing into the duct, which cause a decrease in mass flow to the radiator thus decreasing cooling. 

  With new iteration in development,
